title: Staying Calm When Someone Provokes You
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: Stoic Wisdoms argues that composure under provocation does not mean passively accepting bad treatment. Using Seneca's story of Cato wiping spit from his face and answering with a single dry remark, the essay shows a response that leaves the aggressor responsible for his own behaviour. It draws on Epictetus's habit of telling oneself that a critic is acting on how things seemed to him, and uses the image of lending others pieces of our self-respect to explain why some insults sting. The author distinguishes the involuntary first surge of irritation from the anger we adopt when we accept that we have been wronged and must retaliate. Practical advice follows: learn your own reaction under pressure, pause before answering, ask what you actually want to accomplish, state a boundary and follow through. The essay ends by warning against winning arguments in our heads against opponents who cannot concede.
points: Cato's reply to Lentulus shows that a provoked person can answer on his own terms without needing the other man to grant respect.
Epictetus's reminder that a critic acts on how things seem to him lets you weigh a judgment before deciding whether it deserves a response.
The first flush of irritation is involuntary, but the anger that follows comes from assenting to the idea that we must retaliate, and that assent can be withheld.
Before replying, ask whether there is something to correct, a boundary crossed, or only a wish for the other person to admit fault.
A boundary statement only works if you follow through; announcing that you will leave and then continuing to argue hands control back.
quotes: It’s interesting how little Cato seemed to need from Lentulus. He didn’t attempt to convince the man that he deserved respect, and he had no interest in matching his behavior. He answered the insult in his own way, leaving Lentulus responsible for the disgraceful thing he’d done.
Someone may genuinely believe you’re incompetent, selfish, or deserving of criticism. You can recognize that this is their opinion without immediately feeling compelled to correct it.

I’ve found it useful to think of this as a kind of loan. We allow other people to hold pieces of our self-respect, often without realizing we’ve done it. Their approval makes us feel more confident, and when they withdraw it, we become anxious to win it back.

That’s a useful distinction when you’re the one being provoked. You may not be able to prevent that first surge of irritation, but you can give yourself a chance to regain your composure before responding.

Silence can feel uncomfortable when you’re worried that other people will interpret it as weakness. But you don’t owe everyone an argument about your character, and refusing to participate in a pointless exchange doesn’t mean you’ve agreed with what was said.

The important part is following through. If you announce that you’re leaving and then spend another twenty minutes arguing about why the other person should respect your boundary, you’ve allowed yourself to get drawn back into the exchange. Sometimes the most reasonable thing you can do is end the conversation.
Every round you win in your head is won against an opponent who cannot concede, and the anger refreshes itself each time.
Cato wiped his face and spoke as himself. Someone can provoke you whenever they like, and what they get back is yours to decide.
